memory: Sailing is my other favorite hobby. I grew up in a beautiful marina where my dad brought me sailboats when I was younger. I remember that moment when I felt that rush of wind against the sails, and I was hooked. Now in college, I've tried to keep up with it whenever I go back home for breaks. There's a local sailing club that rents out boats at a decent student rate, so I'll sign up for a day, invite a friend if they want to come, and just spend hours on the water. I love the sense of freedom it gives me. Everything else — Looming deadlines, bug fixes in code, group project drama — just fades into the background. Out there, the water's choppy, the wind's unpredictable, and you've got to keep your head in the game. It's like a puzzle but on a grand scale, which might be why it appeals to my problem-solving nerdy side.Reading is something I feel has been with me since I was a kid. My mom is a huge literature buff, so she used to hand me all these fantasy and sci-fi novels, and I'd find myself lost in other worlds for hours on end. Even now, with a cramped schedule, I try to sneak in some reading before bed or on the weekends when I've got a spare hour. Most recently, I've been obsessed with sci-fi that deals with artificial intelligence — it's partly driven by my academic interests, to be honest. I like imagining future technology and how it might blur boundaries between humans and machines. My favorite AI-themed sci-fi book right now is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. Books like that also help me consider the ethical and social implications of what I'm studying, so in a weird way, reading isn't just relaxation; it's also helping me explore more philosophical questions about the work I'll probably be doing after graduation.Sometimes, I also like to combine hobbies. I’ve had a day where we spent the morning at the lake sailing, then grabbed lunch, then hung out playing video games all evening and talked about how the experience on the water was surprisingly similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. Everyone has a role — whether it’s manning the sails or leading the in-game strategy. That synergy is totally my thing. I love how each hobby, in its own way, demands teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. I’ve also found that scheduling them — just like I schedule study time — helps me keep a healthy balance. For example, every Sunday I’ll look at my week and see if the weather will be nice enough to head to the gym in the afternoon or maybe even drive out to the local lake to spend a few hours on a rented dinghy if I have extra time. If not, I’ll plan an indoor day with friends playing co-op games or doing a workout in my apartment's small fitness center. And reading, well, that’s the easiest to fit in. I’ll do 30 minutes before bedtime, which is such a nice way to wind down from the day. Sometimes, I can read one chapter instead of hours and hours. I can’t sail every weekend, but once a month works. And gaming? Well, if I’ve got 30 minutes to spare, that’s enough to squeeze in a quick match.As a fourth-year Computer Science student, I've been discovering different communities that make campus life feel like a second home. Beyond just coding, I've found various ways to get involved including volunteering, joining clubs, and participating in student activities. I've noticed that campus life is vibrant with so much going on, sometimes it's tough to keep track of everything, but I've learned that community provides a supportive environment.I've been exploring software engineering roles that overlap with the fields I've grown passionate about—data visualization, VR/AR technologies, and maybe some data-driven product development. Over the past couple of years, especially through my research experience, I've discovered this love for making huge datasets approachable and interactive. I keep fantasizing about how that might translate into a commercial product or even an open-source framework that can benefit a wider community. That's one reason I'm drawn to certain tech companies known for pushing boundaries in data analytics or immersive technologies—places like Unity, Unreal, or even some lesser-known startups working on specialized VR solutions for healthcare or engineering. One of my lab mentors basically told me, 'Follow the domain that excites you, not just the biggest name brand out there.' That advice really clicked. Sure, the Googles, Amazons, and Facebooks(or Meta, I guess) of the world are tempting, but so are these smaller companies where I might have a bigger impact earlier on. I've been here for four years, and I always say that as much as I love studying computer science, the people I've met along the way are what really keep me grounded and happy. Ironically, when I first arrived on campus, I thought that making friends might be more challenging—it was my first time living away from home, and I was nervous about whether I'd fit in. But over time, I ended up forming these really tight bonds that, honestly, have made all the stresses and workload of being a CS major feel way more manageable.
